Row.Text: George Washington’s story stitches together multiple threads in American history: loyalty to, and then increasing resentment with, Great Britain; the agricultural South; the industrial North; and the balance between the military and diplomatic faces of the revolution. In his life, he advocated for personal dignity, philosophical liberty, allegiance to the new nation over any personal attachments, and stepping back when his time was finished – Washington was many things, but he would never become a monarch like that which he rebelled against.

Washington was born in 1732 into a modest agricultural family in Virginia, in an era when Virginia was the epitome of a certain kind of colonial subject: British in background, well-educated but fundamentally rural, with an orientation towards the use and application of Enlightenment rationality. Upon his father’s death, his family gave up on formal education, and Washington prepared for a career as a surveyor.

Washington’s estate, like nearly all Southern plantations, used the labor of enslaved Africans. Through the course of his career, though, his attitudes changed (owing in no small part to the influence of the Marquis de Lafayette and Benjamin Franklin), and upon his death he ordered the people he had enslaved to be free. They were – but only after Martha Washington’s death, not his own.

To the west, though, conflicts were brewing. French traders had moved into the Ohio River Valley, lands that were claimed by the British, and Washington became a major in the British forces. His defeat at Fort Necessity began the French and Indian War, a side theater of the larger Seven Years’ War between the French and British.

In this conflict, Washington distinguished himself by his bravery and fortitude, as, in a skirmish at the Monongahela River, two horses were shot out from under him, and he led survivors to safety. But here, the British made a crucial error – they declined to give Washington a commission, sowing the seeds of resentment that were to grow over time.

In peacetime, Washington worked on his estate, planning new agricultural innovations such as crop rotation, switching from tobacco to wheat, and milling flour. Mount Vernon became prosperous as a result…but war was to intrude again.

The Revolution began in the north, but the Americans had remembered Washington’s tenacity and called upon him to command the Continental Army in 1775. As battle raged across the colonies, Washington led the army through surprise attacks, harsh winters and the decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781. Two years later, Washington resigned, his plans for Mount Vernon still front in his mind.
